title: "6. What the models learned, and who they flag"

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4, dpi = 150)
```

```{r load}
source("R/features.R")
source("R/metrics.R")
source("R/models.R")
source("R/decision.R")
source("R/interpret.R")
source("R/imbalance.R")
source("R/plotting.R")
x <- readRDS("data/credit.rds")
cv <- readRDS("results/cv.rds")
tst <- readRDS("results/test.rds")
abl <- readRDS("results/ablation.rds")$behaviour_only
te <- x[cv$is_test, ]
f_te <- build_features(te)
yt <- tst$y
y_tr <- cv$y
logit <- readRDS("results/logit_final.rds")
xgbm <- xgb.load("results/xgb_final.ubj")
X_te <- xgb_matrix(f_te)
shap <- shap_by_feature(xgbm, X_te, feature_groups(f_te))
pct <- function(v, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * v)
f4 <- function(v) sprintf("%.4f", v)
```

Both models are read on the test clients. For the logistic regression, the
contribution of a feature is its term in the log-odds. For XGBoost it is its
SHAP value (Lundberg and Lee, 2017), which splits each prediction, on the
log-odds scale, into a sum of contributions of the features. Both are on the
log-odds scale, but they do not share out the credit in the same way: for an
additive model the centred term is exactly the SHAP value, while for boosted
trees the credit given to correlated features depends on how the trees use
them. The comparisons below are therefore qualitative, about which features
matter and in which direction, not an exact match of importances. Neither
method says anything causal: they describe what the models use, not what makes
a client default.

## Which features matter

```{r logit-contrib}
# contribution of each feature to the log-odds of the logistic regression
b <- as.matrix(coef(logit$fit, s = logit$lambda))[, 1]
lc <- sapply(names(logit$prep), function(fn) {
  Xf <- prep_logit_apply(logit$prep[fn], f_te[fn])
  drop(Xf %*% b[colnames(Xf)])
})
lc <- sweep(lc, 2, colMeans(lc))
kept <- sum(b[-1] != 0)
```

```{r importance, fig.height = 5}
imp <- rbind(
  data.frame(feature = colnames(shap), share = colMeans(abs(shap)) / sum(colMeans(abs(shap))), model = "XGBoost"),
  data.frame(feature = colnames(lc), share = colMeans(abs(lc)) / sum(colMeans(abs(lc))), model = "Logistic regression")
)
ord <- names(sort(tapply(imp$share, imp$feature, mean)))
imp$feature <- factor(imp$feature, levels = ord)
ggplot(imp, aes(share, feature, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = feature), colour = "grey80") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(palette_main[c("accent", "dark")])) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_axis) +
  labs(title = "Share of the average absolute contribution to the log-odds",
       subtitle = "Test set; features of part 1",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_report() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "grey94"))
```

```{r top}
top_x <- names(sort(colMeans(abs(shap)), decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
delinq <- c("delay_1", "max_delay", "months_late", "status_1", "months_no_pay", "worsening")
share_delinq <- sum(colMeans(abs(shap))[delinq]) / sum(colMeans(abs(shap)))
```

The two models agree on what comes first. The delinquency history
(`delay_1`, `max_delay`, `months_late`, `status_1`, `months_no_pay`,
`worsening`) accounts for `r pct(share_delinq, 0)` of XGBoost's contributions.
The credit limit comes next: the bank's own past assessment of the client is one
of the strongest signals available. Beyond these, the logistic regression spreads more weight over the repayment
ratios and utilisation, which carry part of the same information as the
delinquency features, while XGBoost leans more on the delay counts. The lasso
kept `r kept` of the `r length(b) - 1` columns of the logistic
regression, so the penalty mostly shrinks rather than selects.

## The shape of each effect

For the continuous features the logistic regression fits a spline, so its
effects are curves too. The figure compares, for six features, the average
contribution in each decile of the feature, for both models.

```{r shapes, fig.height = 5.2}
feats <- c("log_limit", "util_mean", "repay_mean", "spend_mean", "util_slope", "age")
d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(feats, function(fn) {
  v <- f_te[[fn]]
  bin <- cut(v, unique(quantile(v, seq(0, 1, 0.1))), include.lowest = TRUE)
  rbind(
    data.frame(feature = fn, model = "Logistic regression",
               value = tapply(v, bin, mean), contrib = tapply(lc[, fn], bin, mean)),
    data.frame(feature = fn, model = "XGBoost",
               value = tapply(v, bin, mean), contrib = tapply(shap[, fn], bin, mean))
  )
}))
d$feature <- factor(d$feature, levels = feats)
ggplot(d, aes(value, contrib, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~feature, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(palette_main[c("accent", "dark")])) +
  labs(title = "Contribution to the log-odds of default, by decile of the feature",
       subtitle = "Test set; positive values raise the predicted probability",
       x = NULL, y = "Contribution (log-odds)") +
  theme_report()
```

What the curves say:

- **Credit limit.** The higher the limit, the lower the risk, steadily over the
  whole range. Part of this is the bank's earlier assessment of the client,
  which the model inherits.
- **Utilisation.** A U shape. Accounts that are barely used are riskier than
  those at around 20% of their limit, in line with the higher default rate of
  clients with nothing owed found in part 1. Above that, risk rises with
  utilisation: clients close to their limit have little room left.
- **Repayment ratio.** Both models put most of the effect at the low end:
  repaying only a few percent of the statement is the signal. Beyond that the
  logistic regression keeps rewarding higher repayment while XGBoost is flat,
  presumably because its delinquency features already carry that information.
- **New charges.** Clients who keep adding to their balance are safer, as found
  in part 1, where the reading as a consequence of delinquency rather than a
  cause was discussed.
- **Utilisation trend.** A balance that grows relative to the limit over the
  six months raises the risk.
- **Age.** A small effect: clients in their thirties get the lowest risk, and
  older clients a slightly higher one.

The two models draw broadly the same shapes. XGBoost's advantage in log loss
therefore presumably comes less from different effects than from interactions
between features, which the additive logistic regression cannot represent.

## Personal attributes

Education, marital status and age are inputs; sex is not. Their contribution is
small, and the models lose little without them. Both models were refitted on
account-level and credit-related features only, excluding these three personal
attributes, with the same hyperparameters:

```{r ablation}
L <- function(y, p) -(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p))
set.seed(4)
paired <- function(y, p1, p0, B = 2000) {
  d <- L(y, p1) - L(y, p0)
  q <- quantile(replicate(B, mean(d[sample.int(length(d), replace = TRUE)])), c(0.025, 0.975))
  sprintf("%+.4f [%+.4f, %+.4f]", mean(d), q[1], q[2])
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = c("Logistic regression", "XGBoost"),
  `out of fold, training set` = c(paired(y_tr, abl$oof$logit, tst$oof$logit), paired(y_tr, abl$oof$xgb, tst$oof$xgb)),
  `test set` = c(paired(yt, abl$test$logit, tst$pred$logit), paired(yt, abl$test$xgb, tst$pred$xgb)),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr",
caption = "Change in log loss when education, marital status and age are removed, with 95% paired bootstrap intervals")
```

The loss is about a thousandth of log loss, a tenth of the gap between the two
models. There is also a reason beyond accuracy to drop them. Under the US Equal
Credit Opportunity Act, for example, marital status is a prohibited basis for a
credit decision, and age may enter a scoring system only if elderly applicants
are not assigned a negative value. Here older clients receive a slightly higher
risk than those in their thirties, which would have to be checked against such a
rule. This is one jurisdiction among others, and the rules that applied to
this Taiwanese bank are not assessed here. In general, a model restricted to
account-level and credit-related features is easier to defend, and on this
data it costs almost nothing. It is not free of history either: the credit
limit is itself an earlier decision of the bank.

## Decisions by sex

Sex is not an input, but other features can act as proxies for it. The check is
on the decisions themselves, at the middle cost ratio $r = 0.25$
(threshold `r pct(cost_threshold(0.25), 0)`), for the main model and for the model without personal attributes.

```{r fairness}
t25 <- cost_threshold(0.25)
sex <- ifelse(te$SEX == 1, "men", "women")
group_stats <- function(p) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("men", "women"), function(g) {
    s <- sex == g
    a <- p[s] > t25
    data.frame(
      group = g,
      clients = format(sum(s), big.mark = ","),
      `default rate` = pct(mean(yt[s])),
      `mean prediction` = pct(mean(p[s])),
      `acted on` = pct(mean(a)),
      `good clients acted on` = pct(mean(a[yt[s] == 0])),
      `defaulters caught` = pct(mean(a[yt[s] == 1])),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }))
}
knitr::kable(cbind(model = rep(c("XGBoost", "XGBoost, no personal attributes"), each = 2),
                   rbind(group_stats(tst$pred$xgb), group_stats(abl$test$xgb))),
             row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrrrr")

set.seed(5)
gap <- function(p, B = 2000) {
  a <- p > t25
  stat <- function(i) {
    m <- sex[i] == "men"; good <- yt[i] == 0
    mean(a[i][m & good]) - mean(a[i][!m & good])
  }
  q <- quantile(replicate(B, stat(sample.int(length(yt), replace = TRUE))), c(0.025, 0.975))
  c(est = stat(seq_along(yt)), lo = q[[1]], hi = q[[2]])
}
g_full <- gap(tst$pred$xgb)
g_beh <- gap(abl$test$xgb)
tpr <- tapply(tst$pred$xgb[yt == 1] > t25, sex[yt == 1], mean)
```

The models catch the same share of defaulters among men and women
(`r pct(tpr["men"], 0)` and `r pct(tpr["women"], 0)`). Men who would have
repaid are acted on more often than women who would have repaid: the gap is
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * g_full["est"])` points
(95% interval `r sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", 100 * g_full["lo"], 100 * g_full["hi"])`)
for the main model and `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * g_beh["est"])` points
(`r sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", 100 * g_beh["lo"], 100 * g_beh["hi"])`) without the
personal attributes, so removing them does not close it.

```{r group-calibration}
cal_group <- function(p) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("men", "women"), function(g) {
    s <- sex == g
    est <- calibration_fit(yt[s], p[s])
    bs <- replicate(1000, {
      i <- sample(which(s), replace = TRUE)
      calibration_fit(yt[i], p[i])
    })
    q <- apply(bs, 1, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
    data.frame(group = g,
               intercept = sprintf("%+.2f [%+.2f, %+.2f]", est[1], q[1, 1], q[2, 1]),
               slope = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", est[2], q[1, 2], q[2, 2]))
  }))
}
set.seed(6)
knitr::kable(cal_group(tst$pred$xgb), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr",
             caption = "Calibration intercept and slope of XGBoost within each group, test set, with 95% bootstrap intervals")
```

Within each group the calibration can be checked as in part 3. An intercept
above zero means the model predicts too little default for that group. The
model is not calibrated for men: their intercept is above zero with an interval
that excludes it, so the model slightly underestimates their risk. It is
calibrated for women. The extra false alarms for men therefore do not come from
the model overstating their risk; they come from the larger share of men whose
histories look risky, defaulters or not.

Men in this portfolio default more often (`r pct(mean(yt[sex == "men"]))`
against `r pct(mean(yt[sex == "women"]))`), and their account histories differ.
The observed disparity may reflect differences in base rates and account
histories, but it does not by itself establish that the model is fair or that
the gap is unavoidable. What the literature does establish is a constraint:
when base rates differ, a score that is calibrated within each group cannot
also give equal false positive rates and equal true positive rates
(Chouldechova, 2017; Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, 2017). A bank has to
decide which of these properties to protect, and a gap such as this one is a
reason to investigate which features drive it, not a result to accept as it
stands. Group-specific thresholds would equalise false alarms, but they would
make the decision depend on sex explicitly, which is itself prohibited in many
jurisdictions.

## Limits

- SHAP values and spline terms describe the model, not the clients. A large
  contribution of the credit limit does not mean that raising a limit lowers
  risk.
- The fairness check covers sex only. Age bands and other groups could be
  checked the same way.
- Contributions are averaged over the test set and say little about any single
  client. Explaining an individual decision, as a declined applicant may be
  entitled to, would use the client's own contributions.
